The word breech has a few distinct but related meanings, all of which circle around the same central idea: the back end or rear-bottom part of something. Once you see this thread, every meaning becomes easy to remember.
1. The Rear of a Firearm — the most common modern use

When you look at a gun, it has two ends: the muzzle (the front, where the bullet comes out) and the breech (the back, where the ammunition goes in).

The breech is the rear end of a gun's barrel — the part behind the chamber, where the weapon is loaded. In older guns (called muzzle-loaders), soldiers poured gunpowder and dropped a bullet in from the front. Modern firearms work the opposite way: you load a cartridge or shell from the back, at the breech — which is why modern guns are called breech-loaders.

You've seen this countless times without realizing it. When someone pumps a shotgun, slides the bolt on a rifle, or breaks open a double-barreled gun to drop in two shells — they're accessing the breech to load it.

A few related terms worth knowing:

  • Breech block / Breech bolt — the piece of metal that seals the breech shut when the gun fires, containing the explosion.
  • Breech-loading — describes any firearm loaded from the rear rather than the front.
  • Breech mechanism — the entire system of parts at the rear of a gun that loads, locks, fires, and ejects ammunition.
2. Breech Birth (Medicine) — the second most common use

Normally, a baby in the womb is positioned head-down, so it comes out head-first during birth. But sometimes, a baby is positioned the other way — with its bottom or feet pointing downward, toward the birth canal. This is called a breech presentation or breech birth.

The word here is directly using the older meaning of "breech" as the buttocks or lower rear of the body (explained below). The baby's "breech" — its bottom — is coming first instead of its head.

A breech birth is medically significant because it carries more risk than a head-first delivery. Doctors monitor the baby's position throughout pregnancy, and if a baby is in the breech position close to the due date, the doctor may attempt to turn it manually, plan a C-section, or prepare for a careful vaginal delivery depending on the situation.
3. The Human Buttocks — the oldest meaning

"Breech" was historically used to refer to the buttocks — the lower, rear part of the human body. This meaning is now mostly old-fashioned and rarely used in everyday speech by itself, but it lives on in the medical term breech birth (above) and in the word breeches (below).

You'll often encounter "breeches" (the plural form) as a closely related word. Breeches are a type of trousers that end just below the knee, usually fitted snugly around the thigh and lower leg. They were everyday men's clothing for centuries and are still worn today in equestrian sports (horse riding), historical re-enactments, military ceremonies, and formal court dress in some countries.

The connection: breeches cover the "breech" — the lower body and rear.

You might hear the expression "too big for one's breeches" (sometimes "britches," a casual form), meaning someone is acting with more importance or authority than they actually have — essentially, getting too big for their own pants.

Look at every meaning again:

MeaningWhat "breech" refers to
FirearmThe rear end of the barrel
ChildbirthThe baby's bottom/rear coming first
BodyThe buttocks — rear of the body
BreechesClothing that covers the rear and lower body

In every case, breech = the back, bottom, or rear end of something. That's the concept to hold onto.

These two words sound almost identical and are confused constantly, even by native speakers — so knowing the difference is genuinely useful.

Breech = the rear/back end of something (as above).

Breach = a break, gap, crack, or violation.

  • A breach in a wall — a hole that's been broken through it.
  • A breach of contract — violating the terms of an agreement.
  • A breach of trust — breaking someone's faith in you.
  • A whale breaching — a whale leaping out of the water, breaking through the surface.

They're completely unrelated in meaning. A small trick to keep them apart: "breach" contains the word's idea within its spelling — think of "break" (both start with br and both have the idea of splitting or violating). "Breech" with its double-e (ee) is the one about the rear end.

Breech (noun) refers to the back or rear-bottom part of something — most commonly, the rear end of a gun barrel where ammunition is loaded, and in medicine, a baby positioned bottom-first in the womb. It also has an older meaning of the human buttocks, which is where the word breeches (knee-length trousers) comes from. Do not confuse it with breach, which means a break or violation — a completely different word.
